title: Dispersion & prisms
examples: How does a prism separate colors?
What is the difference between dispersion and scattering?
Can we see a rainbow indoors?

explain.say: When white light enters a prism, it bends into different colors.
Now let me show you the real thing in 3D: a prism splits light. Look at the white light, the prism and the refraction. Tap any part, and I will tell you what it does.
The separation of colors is called dispersion, and it is due to different wavelengths.
A rainbow is a natural example of light dispersion, caused by water droplets.
The blue sky happens because of a process called scattering by the atmosphere.
The scattering effect means that blue light is scattered more than other colors.
In everyday life, a prism or water droplet separates sunlight into its visible spectrum.

faq.a: The sky appears blue because the Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths of light, like blue, more effectively. This is called Rayleigh scattering. It is also known as atmospheric scattering. Some people ask if the atmosphere makes the sun look blue, or what wavelength scatters the most.

Dispersion is the separation of white light into its component colors when it passes through a medium like a prism. This happens because different colors bend at slightly different angles. It is also called chromatic dispersion. Another way to ask is how a prism separates light.
asks: What is the separation of colors?
Does light bend differently by color?

faq.a: A rainbow is formed when sunlight enters spherical water droplets, which refract, reflect, and then disperse the light back to our eyes. This process requires sunlight shining onto falling raindrops. You might also ask about the conditions for a rainbow or how water creates a rainbow.

The visible spectrum is the range of colors that the human eye can detect, arranged in order from red to violet. The order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. You could also ask for the order of colors in light or what colors make up white light.
asks: What are the colors of visible light?
What is the order of colors?
What is the spectrum of visible light?

faq.q: Is dispersion the same as scattering?
faq.a: No, they are different processes. Dispersion specifically refers to the splitting of light by a prism into its constituent colors. Scattering is the general process where light hits particles in the atmosphere and is redirected in many directions. You can ask about the difference between the two or if scattering is always dispersion.
asks: What is the difference between scattering and dispersion?

facts: White light is composed of all the colors of the visible spectrum.
Dispersion separates white light into its component colors.
Blue light scatters more strongly than red light in the atmosphere.
A rainbow is an example of light refracting and reflecting in water droplets.

quiz.say: When white light passes through a prism, which color bends the most?
quiz.why: Violet light has the shortest wavelength, causing it to refract (bend) the most when passing through the prism.

wrong.1: Red light has the longest wavelength, so it bends the least, making it seem like it goes straight through.
wrong.2: Green light is in the middle, so it bends a moderate amount, but not the most.
wrong.3: Blue light bends more than red, but violet bends even more.

quiz.say: What causes the sky to look blue?
quiz.why: The atmosphere's gas molecules scatter shorter wavelengths, like blue, more effectively than longer wavelengths.

wrong.0: Raindrops cause dispersion, but the blue sky effect is due to scattering by gas molecules.
wrong.2: The sun emits all colors, not just blue; the blue appearance is due to scattering.
wrong.3: Prisms are solid objects; the scattering happens due to tiny particles in the air.

quiz.say: If you see a rainbow, what natural phenomenon is happening?
quiz.why: A rainbow requires light to bend (refract), bounce off (reflect), and split (disperse) inside water droplets.

wrong.0: Scattering alone only explains the blue sky, not the full spectrum of a rainbow.
wrong.1: Dispersion only describes the splitting; the reflection and initial bending are also key.
wrong.2: Refraction describes the initial bend, but the light must also reflect and disperse to form a rainbow.
